content: Mortality rates associated with sepsis and septic shock remain alarmingly high. Clinical trials investigating the use of intravenous immunoglobulins (IVIG) as an adjunctive treatment for sepsis have yielded inconsistent results. This review represents an updated analysis of a Cochrane review originally published in 1999, with subsequent updates in 2002 and 2010. The primary objective of this review was to evaluate the effects of IVIG as an adjunctive therapy in patients with bacterial sepsis or septic shock, specifically focusing on mortality rates, bacteriological failure rates, and the duration of hospital stays. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE, and EMBASE, covering studies up to December 2012. Investigators in the field were also contacted to obtain unpublished data. The original search was performed in 1999, with updates in 2002 and 2008. The review included randomized controlled trials that compared IVIG (either monoclonal or polyclonal) with placebo or no intervention in patients of any age diagnosed with bacterial sepsis or septic shock. Two independent authors assessed the studies for inclusion, evaluated their methodological quality, and extracted relevant data. Pre-specified subgroup analyses were conducted based on the type of immunoglobulin preparation. Out of 88 potentially eligible studies, 43 met the inclusion criteria for this updated review. Among these, a large trial on polyclonal IVIG in neonates, which concluded in 2011, was included. Due to clinical heterogeneity, pooled analysis of polyclonal and monoclonal IVIG was not performed. Subgroup analysis of 10 trials involving polyclonal IVIG (n = 1430) and seven trials on IgM-enriched polyclonal IVIG (n = 528) demonstrated significant reductions in mortality among adults with sepsis when compared to placebo or no intervention. The relative risk (RR) for polyclonal IVIG was 0.81 (95% confidence interval [CI] 0.70 to 0.93), and for IgM-enriched polyclonal IVIG, the RR was 0.66 (95% CI 0.51 to 0.85). In contrast, subgroup analysis of polyclonal IVIG in neonates, which included the recently concluded large trial, showed no significant reduction in mortality. For standard IVIG, the RR was 1.00 (95% CI 0.92 to 1.08; five trials, n = 3667), and for IgM-enriched polyclonal IVIG, the RR was 0.57 (95% CI 0.31 to 1.04; three trials, n = 164). Sensitivity analysis of trials with a low risk of bias revealed no reduction in mortality with polyclonal IVIG in adults (RR 0.97; 95% CI 0.81 to 1.15; five trials, n = 945) or neonates (RR 1.01; 95% CI 0.93 to 1.09; three trials, n = 3561). Furthermore, mortality was not reduced among patients who received anti-endotoxin antibodies (eight trials, n = 4671; RR 0.99; 95% CI 0.91 to 1.06). Anti-cytokine therapies demonstrated a marginal reduction in mortality (nine trials, n = 7893; RR 0.92; 95% CI 0.86 to 0.97). In conclusion, polyclonal IVIG was associated with reduced mortality in adults with sepsis; however, this benefit was not observed in trials with a low risk of bias. Among neonates with sepsis, there is sufficient evidence to conclude that standard polyclonal IVIG does not reduce mortality, as demonstrated by the inclusion of the large neonatal trial. For IgM-enriched IVIG, the available trials in both neonates and adults were small, and the evidence remains insufficient to draw robust conclusions regarding its benefit. The use of monoclonal IVIG as adjunctive therapy remains experimental.
